questions.q: What is execArgv on child_process.fork() or spawn()?
o: The working directory path given to the child process
An array of Node CLI flags passed to the child at startup
The environment block the child inherits from the parent
The maximum heap size the child is allowed to allocate
questions.x: execArgv is an array of strings such as ["--inspect"] or ["--eval=console.log(1)"]. Those are the same kind of flags you would type before a script name when starting Node yourself. It is not the child's env block and it is not a shell command string.
questions.h: Think of flags you pass to the node binary itself, before the script path. fork and spawn can pass that same list through one options field.

questions.q: Why can Object.prototype.execArgv affect fork() or spawn()?
o: fork() always treats execArgv values as shell command strings
A missing own execArgv is read from the prototype chain on options
execArgv replaces the running Node binary with a new version
Object.prototype is sealed, so inherited flags cannot be ignored
questions.x: If code builds an options object and never sets execArgv, a normal property read still walks the prototype chain. After Object.prototype.execArgv = ["--eval=..."], options.execArgv is that array. The gadget is not 'fork is always RCE'. It is polluted execArgv plus a fork or spawn call whose options inherit that value.
questions.h: The options object has no own execArgv. Where else does a JavaScript property read look?

questions.q: Which Node flag is the useful execArgv gadget for running attacker code?
o: --version, which prints the Node release string and then exits
--eval or -e, which runs JavaScript while the child is booting
--help, which writes the usage text to stdout and then exits
--max-old-space-size, which only raises or lowers the heap limit
questions.x: --eval makes the child run attacker JavaScript during startup. From that JavaScript you can call require("child_process").execSync(...) and run OS commands. --inspect and --require also change boot, but --eval is the one that runs inline code.
questions.h: You need a flag that executes JavaScript before the worker script loads. Which node flag is the one-liner for that?

questions.q: On which Node.js versions did inherited execArgv still work as a gadget?
o: All current Node.js releases, including every latest LTS build
Node before 18.18.0 and 20.6.0, which still read inherited options
Only Node.js 4.x, and only if the process is started with -r
Only Windows builds, because they resolve flags via cmd.exe
questions.x: Before 18.18.0 and 20.6.0, child_process honored execArgv found on the options prototype chain. Those releases started honoring only own properties, so a polluted Object.prototype.execArgv is ignored. The gadget is still about fork and spawn options, not about env._ or shell:true.
questions.h: A Node fix stopped treating inherited options as real flags. Which version cutoff is that change?

questions.q: What is the execArgv gadget, as opposed to a shell or env._ gadget?
o: Polluting env._ so a child shell expands that value as a command
Polluting execArgv, then calling fork or spawn with inherited options
Setting shell:true so spawn joins arguments through /bin/sh -c
Writing NODE_OPTIONS into process.env from a polluted env object
questions.x: env._, shell:true, and NODE_OPTIONS are different prototype-pollution gadgets. This one is: pollute execArgv, then hit code that calls fork or spawn with an options object that inherits that array. The child Node process then boots with attacker CLI flags such as --eval.
questions.h: The options field is named execArgv and it holds Node CLI flags. It is not the shell string and it is not env._.
